learning_objective: 🎯 Understand smooth, unbroken math curves and learn how to calculate their exact rate of change at any single split-second point!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: A function is continuous if you can draw its graph on a piece of paper without ever lifting your pen. Mathematically, the Left Hand Limit, Right Hand Limit, and the value at the point must all be exactly equal.
Differentiability is finding the derivative. A derivative is just a fancy word for the exact slope or 'rate of change' of a curve at one specific microscopic point.

When a function is stuffed inside another function (like Russian nesting dolls), you use the Chain Rule. You differentiate the outside function first, then multiply it by the derivative of the inside function.

Sometimes x and y are mixed up so badly in an equation that you can't isolate y. You differentiate both sides with respect to x as they are, remembering to attach a 'dy/dx' whenever you differentiate a y term.

fun_activity.title: 🎢 The Rollercoaster Check
fun_activity.instructions: Look at a picture of a rollercoaster track. Identify 'continuous' sections (smooth track). Now identify points where the track suddenly sharply changes direction (corners). Those sharp corners are continuous, but NOT differentiable!

exam_tips: 📌 'Differentiability implies Continuity, but Continuity does NOT imply Differentiability.' (Think of a sharp V-shape curve: it's unbroken, but doesn't have a defined slope at the sharp point).
📌 For Logarithmic Differentiation, always take 'log' on both sides FIRST when you see a function raised to the power of another function, like $x^x$.
📌 Don't skip the 'dy/dx' when differentiating 'y' terms in implicit equations—it is the most common student mistake.
quick_recap: ⭐ LHL = RHL = f(a) is the golden rule for proving continuity.
⭐ Use the Chain Rule carefully from the outside in.
⭐ Parametric functions require you to differentiate x and y separately, then divide them.
